points.title: Every noun has a gender
points.short: masculine, feminine or neuter — you can usually tell from the ending
points.explain:
In Slovenian every noun is **masculine (m)**, **feminine (ž)** or **neuter (s)**. This isn't about meaning — a chair is masculine and a house is feminine — but it matters a lot, because adjectives, words like "my" and later the case endings all change with the gender.

The good news: in most cases the **last letter** of the word tells you the gender:
• ends in a **consonant** → usually masculine: stol, kruh, avto (exception: avto, kino, radio end in -o but are masculine)
• ends in **-a** → usually feminine: hiš[a], kav[a], mam[a]
• ends in **-o** or **-e** → usually neuter: mest[o], mlek[o], morj[e], sonc[e]

A few useful exceptions to keep in mind: words for men are masculine even when they end in -a or -e (oče, ati, vodja), and some feminine words end in a consonant (noč, pot, sol, stvar, jesen).

In the app you'll see a small tag next to every noun: **m**, **ž** or **s**. Say the word together with its gender in your head ("ta hiša, ta stol, to mesto") and the gender will stick by itself.

points.title: To be: sem, si, je …
points.short: the verb "to be" in the present
points.explain:
**Biti** (to be) is the most important verb. In the present tense it looks like this:
• jaz [sem] — I am
• ti [si] — you are (one person, informal)
• on / ona / ono [je] — he / she / it is
• mi [smo] — we are
• vi [ste] — you are (several people, or formal)
• oni / one [so] — they are

Slovenian also has a form for **two people** (the dual): midva [sva] (we two), vidva [sta] (you two), onadva [sta] (they two). You'll meet it properly later.

Because the verb ending already shows **who** is meant, the pronoun is usually **left out**: "[Sem] Ana." is more natural than "Jaz sem Ana." Use the pronoun only to stress it: "Jaz sem iz Slovenije, ti pa iz Italije."

These short forms are "lazy" little words: they like to stand in **second place** in the sentence — "Danes [sem] doma." (Today I am at home.) — not at the very end or very beginning.

points.title: I, you, he, she …
points.pattern: jaz · ti · on · ona · ono · mi · vi · oni · one
points.short: personal pronouns — and when to drop them
points.explain:
The personal pronouns in Slovenian:
• **jaz** — I
• **ti** — you (one person you know well)
• **on** — he · **ona** — she · **ono** — it (for neuter things)
• **mi** — we
• **vi** — you (several people — or one person, politely)
• **oni** — they (men, or a mixed group) · **one** — they (only women or only feminine things)

Two things are different from English:

**1. "It" follows the gender.** A chair (stol, m) is **on**, a house (hiša, ž) is **ona**, a town (mesto, s) is **ono**: "Kje je hiša? Ona je tam." — "Where is the house? It is there."

**2. Pronouns are usually dropped.** The verb ending already says who does it: "Govori[m] slovensko." = I speak Slovenian. You add the pronoun only for emphasis or contrast: "**Jaz** pijem kavo, **on** pa čaj."

examples.text: On je učitelj, ona je zdravnica.
examples.en: He is a teacher, she is a doctor.

examples.text: Kje je hiša? Ona je tam.
examples.en: Where is the house? It is over there.

points.title: Saying no: nisem, ni, ne
points.short: negative of "to be" and of other verbs
points.explain:
To make a sentence negative, Slovenian uses **ne** before the verb: "Ne razumem." (I don't understand.) "Ne pijem kave." (I don't drink coffee.)

The verb **biti** is special: "ne" melts together with it into one word:
• sem → [nisem] (I am not)
• si → [nisi]
• je → [ni]
• smo → [nismo]
• ste → [niste]
• so → [niso]

So you say "[Nisem] utrujen." (I'm not tired), never "ne sem". The same happens with **imeti** (to have): imam → **nimam** (I don't have) — more about that later.

A handy short answer: "Ne, hvala." (No, thanks.) And to say something is not there: "Kave [ni]." (There's no coffee.)

points.title: Asking questions
points.short: yes/no questions with ali, and question words
points.explain:
**Yes/no questions** are easy: keep the normal word order and either raise your voice at the end, or put **ali** at the beginning (a bit more careful, written style):
• "Si utrujen?" or "**Ali** si utrujen?" — Are you tired?
• "Ali govoriš angleško?" — Do you speak English?

**Question words** go at the beginning:
• **kdo** — who · **kaj** — what
• **kje** — where (location) · **kam** — where to · **od kod** — where from
• **kdaj** — when · **kako** — how · **zakaj** — why
• **koliko** — how much / how many

Note that Slovenian separates **kje** (where something is) and **kam** (where you're going): "Kje si?" (Where are you?) but "Kam greš?" (Where are you going?). This difference will matter a lot when you learn cases.

Polite request: "Ali mi lahko pomagate?" — Can you help me?

examples.en: How much does the coffee cost?

points.title: Verbs like delati: -am, -aš, -a
points.pattern: dela[m] · dela[š] · dela · dela[mo] · dela[te] · dela[jo]
points.short: present tense of verbs ending in -am
points.explain:
Slovenian verbs change their ending for each person. Good news: there are only **three main patterns**, named after the "I" form: **-am**, **-im** and **-em**.

The first group is **-am** verbs, like **delati** (to work, to do). Take the stem **dela-** and add:
• (jaz) dela[m] — I work
• (ti) dela[š] — you work
• (on/ona) dela — he/she works (no ending!)
• (mi) dela[mo] — we work
• (vi) dela[te] — you work
• (oni) dela[jo] — they work

For two people (dual): dela[va] (we two), dela[ta] (you two / they two).

Other -am verbs you know: imeti → ima[m], gledati → gleda[m], poslušati → posluša[m], čakati → čaka[m], kuhati → kuha[m], igrati → igra[m], vprašati → vpraša[m], plačati → plača[m], pomagati → pomaga[m], poznati → pozna[m].

Remember: there is no separate "am doing" form. "Dela[m]" means both "I work" and "I am working".

points.title: Verbs like govoriti: -im, -iš, -i
points.pattern: govori[m] · govori[š] · govori · govori[mo] · govori[te] · govori[jo]
points.short: present tense of verbs ending in -im
points.explain:
The second group of verbs has **-i-** before the endings. The model verb is **govoriti** (to speak). Stem **govori-**, then the same endings as before:
• govori[m] — I speak
• govori[š] — you speak
• govori — he/she speaks
• govori[mo] — we speak
• govori[te] — you speak
• govori[jo] — they speak

Dual: govori[va], govori[ta].

The endings are exactly the same as for -am verbs (-m, -š, –, -mo, -te, -jo) — only the vowel before them is **i** instead of **a**. So once you know one group, you almost know the other.

Other -im verbs: videti → vidi[m], živeti → živi[m], misliti → misli[m], kupiti → kupi[m], želeti → želi[m], učiti se → uči[m] se, sedeti → sedi[m], voziti → vozi[m], ljubiti → ljubi[m], spati → spi[m] (this one is a bit irregular).

Tip: in the dictionary form (infinitive) you can't always see the group — that's why the app shows the "I" form in brackets: "videti (vidim)".

points.title: Verbs like pisati: -em, -eš, -e
points.pattern: piše[m] · piše[š] · piše · piše[mo] · piše[te] · piše[jo]
points.short: present tense of verbs ending in -em (and grem)
points.explain:
The third group has **-e-** before the endings: same endings, new vowel. But here the **stem often changes** a little compared to the infinitive, so it pays to learn the "I" form with each verb:
• pisati → piše[m] (I write), piše[š], piše, piše[mo], piše[te], piše[jo]
• brati → bere[m] (I read)
• iti → gre[m] (I go)
• priti → pride[m] (I come)
• piti → pije[m] (I drink)
• razumeti → razume[m] (I understand)
• hoteti → hoče[m] (I want)
• iskati → išče[m] (I look for)
• potovati → potuje[m] (I travel) — all verbs in **-ovati** become **-ujem**

The endings, once more: -m, -š, nothing, -mo, -te, -jo. Dual: -va, -ta.

A few very common verbs are completely irregular and simply have to be learned: **jesti** → jem, ješ, je, jemo, jeste, jedo; **vedeti** → vem, veš, ve, vemo, veste, vedo; **dati** → dam, daš, da, damo, daste, dajo.

examples.en: In the evening I read a book.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside.

points.title: To have: imam — and nimam
points.short: the verb "to have" and its negative
points.explain:
**Imeti** (to have) is a regular -am verb:
• ima[m] — I have
• ima[š] — you have
• ima — he/she has
• ima[mo] — we have
• ima[te] — you have
• ima[jo] — they have

Its negative melts together, like with biti: **ne + imam = nimam**:
• [nimam], [nimaš], [nima], [nimamo], [nimate], [nimajo]

Imeti is used in many everyday phrases where English uses other verbs:
• Age: "Star sem dvajset let." or "Imam dvajset let." (I'm twenty.)
• "Imam rad kavo." — I like coffee (literally: I have coffee dear) — rad changes to **rada** if you're a woman.
• "Imam čas." — I have time. → "Nimam časa." — I don't have time.

Watch that last pair: after **nimam** the noun changes its ending (čas → čas[a]). That's the genitive case, which comes in a later lesson — for now just notice it.

examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.
We have a dog and a cat.

points.title: Adjectives agree: nov stol, nov[a] hiša, nov[o] mesto
points.pattern: nov stol · nov[a] hiša · nov[o] mesto
points.short: adjectives take the gender of their noun
points.explain:
An adjective (big, new, beautiful …) always takes the **same gender as its noun**. In the dictionary you see the masculine form, and you change the ending:
• masculine: **nov** stol — (no ending, or -i: novi)
• feminine: **nov[a]** hiša — ending **-a**
• neuter: **nov[o]** mesto — ending **-o** (after č, š, ž, c, j it's **-e**: vroč[e] sonce)

So the adjective "rhymes" with the noun: lep[a] hiš[a], lep[o] mest[o].

Many adjectives lose a vowel when they get an ending: **majhen** → majhn[a] hiša, majhn[o] okno; **dober** → dobr[a] kava; **topel** → topl[a] voda; **lačen** → lačn[a]. Don't worry — you'll get used to it by hearing it.

The same endings appear when the adjective comes after "to be": "Hiša je velik[a]." "Mesto je lep[o]." And if you're a woman, adjectives about you are feminine: "Utrujen[a] sem." (I'm tired — said by a woman.)

Also note: **to je** (this is) never changes: "To je nova hiša."

points.title: My, your: moj, moj[a], moj[e]
points.pattern: moj brat · moj[a] sestra · moj[e] ime
points.short: possessive words change like adjectives
points.explain:
Words like **my, your, his** behave exactly like adjectives — they take the gender of the **thing owned** (not of the owner!):
• **moj** brat · moj[a] sestra · moj[e] ime — my
• **tvoj** · tvoj[a] · tvoj[e] — your (informal)
• **njegov** · njegov[a] · njegov[o] — his
• **njen** · njen[a] · njen[o] — her
• **naš** · naš[a] · naš[e] — our
• **vaš** · vaš[a] · vaš[e] — your (plural / formal)

Notice that after **j** and **š** the neuter ending is **-e** (moj[e], naš[e]), after other letters it's **-o** (njegov[o], njen[o]).

The important difference from English: "his sister" and "her sister" use different words (njegova / njena) — but the ending (-a) comes from **sestra**, which is feminine. Think: "whose?" chooses the word, "what?" chooses the ending.

"Čigav je ta avto?" — Whose car is this? "To je moj avto."

points.title: More than two: stol[i], hiš[e], mest[a]
points.pattern: stol → stol[i] · hiša → hiš[e] · mesto → mest[a]
points.short: plural of nouns (3 or more)
points.explain:
For **three or more** things, nouns get a plural ending (for exactly two there's a special form — the dual — in another lesson):
• masculine: + **-i** → stol → stol[i], brat → brat[je] (a few use -je: brat, mož)
• feminine: -a → **-e** → hiš[a] → hiš[e], knjig[a] → knjig[e]
• neuter: -o/-e → **-a** → mest[o] → mest[a], morj[e] → morj[a]

So the plural endings are just three: **-i, -e, -a**. Yes, that means neuter plural ends in -a — just like feminine singular. The gender tag helps you not mix them up.

Adjectives follow in the plural too: nov[i] stol[i], nov[e] hiš[e], nov[a] mest[a].

Some masculine nouns add **-ov-** before the plural ending (mostly short words): grad → grad[ovi], most → most[ovi], sin → sin[ovi].

Some common nouns only exist in the plural (marked **mn** in the app): vrata (door), hlače (trousers), starši (parents), počitnice (holidays) — "Vrata so odprta." (The door is open.)

examples.en: There are three chairs in the room.
There are books on the table.

points.title: Polite "you": vikanje
points.short: use vi (plural forms) for strangers and older people
points.explain:
Slovenian has two ways of saying "you" to one person:
• **tikanje** — using **ti**: with friends, family, children, and young people among themselves.
• **vikanje** — using **vi**: with strangers, in shops and offices, with older people, teachers, your boss.

When you say **vi** to one person, the verb goes in the **plural** form: "Kako [ste]?" (How are you?), "Ali govori[te] angleško?", "Od kod [ste]?"

Greetings and words change too: **živjo / oprosti** (informal) vs **dober dan / oprostite** (polite). "Prosim" works with everybody.

When in doubt, use **vi**. If the other person wants to switch, they'll say "Lahko se tikava." (We can say "ti" to each other.)

examples.en: Excuse me, do you speak English?

points.title: What do you see? Feminine -a → -o
points.short: accusative (tožilnik) of feminine nouns
points.explain:
Now the big topic of Slovenian: **cases** (skloni). A noun changes its ending depending on its **role in the sentence**. Don't panic — we'll take them one at a time, starting with the most useful one.

The **accusative** (tožilnik) is used for the **object** — the thing you see, have, buy, drink, want, love: "I drink **coffee**", "I see **a house**".

For **feminine nouns in -a** the rule is simple: **-a becomes -o**.
• kav[a] → Pijem kav[o]. (I drink coffee.)
• hiš[a] → Vidim hiš[o]. (I see a house.)
• sestr[a] → Imam sestr[o]. (I have a sister.)
• voda → "Vod[o], prosim." (Water, please.)

Adjectives and words like "my" do the same: "Imam nov[o] knjig[o]." "Kličem moj[o] mam[o]."

Feminine nouns ending in a consonant (noč, sol, pot) **don't change** in the accusative: "Daj mi sol."

This is also the form you use when you order something: "Kav[o] z mlekom, prosim." — so you'll use it every day.

points.title: Accusative of masculine and neuter
points.pattern: Vidim stol. · Vidim brat[a]. · Pijem mlek[o].
points.short: things don't change; people and animals add -a
points.explain:
In the accusative, **masculine** nouns have one rule that depends on whether the noun is **alive**:
• **things** (not alive): **no change** — "Jem kruh." "Imam avto." "Vidim stol."
• **people and animals**: add **-a** — brat → "Imam brat[a]." pes → "Imam ps[a]." prijatelj → "Čakam prijatelj[a]."

(Notice pes → ps[a]: some words lose their -e- when they get an ending, like we saw with adjectives.)

**Neuter** nouns never change in the accusative: "Pijem mleko." "Vidim morje." "Imam stanovanje."

Adjectives follow the same idea: a masculine thing keeps its form ("Imam nov avto."), a masculine person gets **-ega**: "Imam star[ega] brat[a]." — that's a longer ending, but you'll hear it often.

Summary of the accusative so far:
• ž: hiš[a] → hiš[o]
• m (thing): stol → stol
• m (alive): brat → brat[a]
• s: mesto → mesto

examples.en: I eat bread and drink milk.

points.title: Where to? Grem v šol[o] · na pošt[o]
points.short: v / na + accusative for the place you're going to
points.explain:
When you go **somewhere** (question **kam?** — where to?), Slovenian uses **v** or **na** + the **accusative** — the same endings you just learned:
• Grem v šol[o]. — I'm going to school. (šola → šolo)
• Grem v trgovin[o]. — I'm going to the shop.
• Grem na pošt[o]. — I'm going to the post office.
• Gremo na morje. — We're going to the seaside. (neuter: no change)
• Grem v park. — I'm going to the park. (masculine thing: no change)

**v or na?** Roughly: **v** = into a closed space or a town/country (v šolo, v trgovino, v Ljubljano, v Italijo); **na** = onto a surface, open places, events and some fixed words (na pošto, na postajo, na morje, na koncert, na avtobus, na Bled). Some just have to be learned with the word — the app's examples help.

Two important exceptions that don't use v/na: **domov** (home): "Grem domov." and **k** + person (to someone's place) — that's a different case, coming later.

examples.en: I'm going to the post office.
In summer we go to the seaside.

points.title: Where? Sem v šol[i] · na pošt[i]
points.short: v / na + locative (mestnik) for where something is
points.explain:
When something **is** somewhere (question **kje?** — where?), Slovenian uses **v** or **na** + a new case, the **locative** (mestnik). The locative is only ever used after prepositions, so it's easy to spot.

The endings:
• feminine -a → **-i**: šol[a] → v šol[i], pošt[a] → na pošt[i], Ljubljan[a] → v Ljubljan[i]
• masculine → **-u**: hotel → v hotel[u], park → v park[u], avtobus → na avtobus[u]
• neuter → **-u**: mest[o] → v mest[u], morj[e] → na morj[u]

Compare the pair that confuses everyone at first:
• Kam greš? → **Grem** v šol[o]. (movement → accusative, -o)
• Kje si? → **Sem** v šol[i]. (location → locative, -i)

Same little word "v", different ending — the ending carries the meaning "to" or "in". The same choice of v / na applies as before: v šoli, na pošti, na morju, v Ljubljani, na Bledu.

Other prepositions with the locative: **pri** (at someone's / near): pri mam[i] (at mom's); **o** (about): "Govorimo o film[u]."; **po** (after / around): po kosil[u] (after lunch).

examples.en: In summer we're at the seaside.
After lunch I go for a walk.

points.title: Nimam čas[a]: the genitive after "no"
points.short: genitive (rodilnik) after nimam, ni, brez
points.explain:
The **genitive** (rodilnik) has many uses. The first one is with **negation**: when you say you **don't have** something, or something **isn't there**, the noun goes into the genitive.

The endings:
• feminine -a → **-e**: kav[a] → "Nimam kav[e]." (I have no coffee.)
• masculine → **-a**: čas → "Nimam čas[a]." kruh → "Ni kruh[a]." (There's no bread.)
• neuter -o/-e → **-a**: mlek[o] → "Ni mlek[a]."

So with negation, compare:
• Imam sestr[o]. → Nimam sestr[e].
• Vidim avto. → Ne vidim avt[a].
• Tukaj je park. → Tukaj ni park[a].

The genitive also comes after the preposition **brez** (without): "Kava brez sladkorj[a]" (coffee without sugar), "čaj brez mlek[a]", and after **iz** and **od** (from): "Sem iz Slovenij[e]." (I'm from Slovenia.), "od mam[e]" (from mom), and after **do** (until, to): "do pošt[e]".

examples.en: There's no milk in the fridge.

points.title: Veliko vod[e], kilogram kruh[a]
points.short: genitive after amounts and quantity words
points.explain:
The second big use of the **genitive**: after words of **amount**. When English says "a glass **of** water", Slovenian puts "water" in the genitive (no extra word for "of"):
• kozarec vod[e] — a glass of water
• skodelica kav[e] — a cup of coffee
• kilogram kruh[a] — a kilo of bread
• liter mlek[a] — a litre of milk
• kos torte → kos tort[e] — a piece of cake

The same after **veliko** (a lot), **malo** (a little), **dovolj** (enough), **več** (more), **koliko** (how much):
• Imam veliko del[a]. — I have a lot of work.
• Koliko denarj[a] imaš? — How much money do you have?

For things you count, the **genitive plural** is used after these words and after numbers from 5 up. Its endings: masculine **-ov** (stol → pet stol[ov]), feminine and neuter mostly **no ending** (hiša → pet hiš, jabolko → kilogram jabolk). "Veliko ljudi" (a lot of people) is an irregular one worth remembering.

examples.en: I have a lot of work.
How much money do you have?
A kilo of apples costs two euros.

points.title: 1 stol, 2 stol[a], 3 stol[i], 5 stol[ov]
points.pattern: en stol · dva stol[a] · trije stol[i] · pet stol[ov]
points.short: the noun changes with the number
points.explain:
Counting in Slovenian has a special logic, because the noun changes with the number:
• **1** → singular: en stol, ena hiša, eno jabolko
• **2** → dual: dva stol[a], dve hiš[i], dve jabolk[i]
• **3 and 4** → plural: trije stol[i], tri hiš[e], štiri jabolk[a]
• **5 and more** → genitive plural: pet stol[ov], pet hiš, pet jabolk

Numbers 1–4 also change with gender:
• 1: en (m), ena (ž), eno (s)
• 2: dva (m), dve (ž, s)
• 3: trije (m), tri (ž, s)
• 4: štirje (m), štiri (ž, s)
From 5 on, numbers don't change: pet, šest, sedem …

Prices work the same way: en evro, dva evr[a], trije evr[i], pet evr[ov]. "Koliko stane?" — "Tri evre." (in the accusative, "trije" becomes "tri").

It sounds like a lot, but you'll mostly hear the pattern 1 / 2 / 3–4 / 5+, and after a while it just sounds right.

examples.en: There are five students in the class.
There are three books on the table.

points.title: Exactly two: the dual (dvojina)
points.short: Slovenian's special form for two
points.explain:
Here is something that makes Slovenian special: besides singular (1) and plural (3+) it has a **dual** (dvojina) — a separate form for **exactly two**. Very few languages in the world still use it!

**Pronouns and "to be":**
• **midva** (we two, m) / **medve** (we two, ž) → [sva]: "Midva [sva] prijatelja."
• **vidva / vidve** (you two) → [sta]
• **onadva / onidve** (they two) → [sta]

**Verbs** in the dual end in **-va** (we two) and **-ta** (you two / they two):
• dela[va], dela[ta] · govori[va], govori[ta] · gre[va], gre[ta]

**Nouns** after "dva / dve":
• masculine: + **-a** → dva stol[a], dva brat[a]
• feminine: -a → **-i** → dve hiš[i], dve sestr[i]
• neuter: → **-i** → dve mest[i], dve jabolk[i]

It's used all the time, especially for couples and pairs: "Kam gre[va]?" (Where are we two going?), "Ali sta utrujena?" (Are you two tired?). If you say plural instead of dual, people will understand you — but using the dual will make you sound really Slovenian.

examples.en: There are two glasses on the table.

points.title: With: kava z mlek[om], grem z mam[o]
points.short: s / z + instrumental (orodnik)
points.explain:
To say **with**, Slovenian uses **z** or **s** + the **instrumental** case (orodnik):
• masculine and neuter → **-om** (after č, š, ž, c, j: **-em**): z mlek[om], s sladkorj[em], s prijatelj[em], z avtom
• feminine -a → **-o**: z mam[o], s sestr[o], s kartic[o]

**z or s?** Use **s** before the voiceless sounds **c, č, f, h, k, p, s, š, t** (s sestro, s kartico, s prijateljem, s teto), and **z** before everything else (z mamo, z mlekom, z avtobusom). Say it out loud and it chooses itself — it's just pronunciation.

Typical uses:
• company: "Grem v kino s prijatelj[em]." (with a friend)
• food: "kava z mlek[om]", "čaj z limon[o]"
• transport: "Grem z avtobus[om] / z vlak[om] / z avt[om]." (by bus, train, car)
• paying: "Plačam s kartic[o]." (I'll pay by card.)

Notice: feminine instrumental (-o) looks just like feminine accusative (-o). The preposition z/s tells you which one it is.

examples.en: I'm going to the cinema with a friend.
I go to work by bus.
I live with my mom and sister.

points.title: To someone: Dam mam[i], grem k brat[u]
points.short: dative (dajalnik): giving, telling, going to a person
points.explain:
The **dative** (dajalnik) answers **komu?** — to whom? You use it for the person who **receives** something: you give, send, tell, show, help **someone**.

Endings:
• feminine -a → **-i**: mam[a] → "Dam mam[i] darilo." (I give mom a present.)
• masculine and neuter → **-u**: brat → "Pišem brat[u]." (I'm writing to my brother.)

Verbs with the dative: **dati** (give), **reči / povedati** (say, tell), **pisati** (write to), **pokazati** (show), **pomagati** (help) — careful, in Slovenian you help **to** someone: "Pomagam sosed[u]." (I help the neighbour.)

The preposition **k** (before k and g it becomes **h**) + dative means **to someone's place**: "Grem k mam[i]." (I'm going to mom's.), "Grem k zdravnik[u]." (I'm going to the doctor.), "Grem h Gorazd[u]."

You'll also meet the dative in feelings: "Mraz mi je." (I'm cold — literally: to me is cold.), "Všeč mi je." (I like it.) — **mi** is the short dative of jaz; **ti** = to you, **mu** = to him, **ji** = to her.

examples.en: Tomorrow I'm going to the doctor.

points.title: I like to: rad / rad[a] + verb
points.short: rad / rada / radi + verb = to like doing
points.explain:
To say you **like doing** something, put **rad** before the verb — literally "gladly":
• "Rad berem." — I like reading. (said by a man)
• "Rad[a] berem." — I like reading. (said by a woman)
• "Rad[i] potujemo." — We like travelling. (a group)

**Rad** changes like an adjective — it agrees with **who** likes: rad (m), rad[a] (ž), rad[i] (m plural), rad[e] (ž plural), rad[a] / rad[i] in the dual (midva rada).

The word order is usually: (subject) + **rad** + verb: "Ana rada pleše." "Ali rad kuhaš?"

To like **a thing**, use **imeti rad**: "Rad imam kavo." (I like coffee.) or the more neutral **všeč**: "Kava mi je všeč." (I like the coffee — it's pleasing to me.)

Negative: "Ne berem rad." (I don't like reading.) — "ne" goes before the verb, and rad moves after it.

The opposite of rad is **nerad**: "Nerad vstajam zgodaj." (I don't like getting up early.)

examples.en: Do you like travelling? (to a group)

points.title: Must, can, want: moram, lahko, hočem
points.pattern: Moram delati. · Lahko pridem. · Hočem spati.
points.short: modal verbs + infinitive
points.explain:
Some verbs are followed by another verb in its **dictionary form** (infinitive, ending in **-ti** or **-či**):
• **morati** (must, have to) → "Moram delati." (I have to work.)
• **hoteti** (want) → "Hočem spati." (I want to sleep.)
• **želeti** (wish, would like — more polite) → "Želim plačati." (I'd like to pay.)
• **znati** (know how to) → "Znam plavati." (I can swim.)

**Can / may** is usually expressed with the little word **lahko** + the normal present tense: "Lahko pridem jutri." (I can come tomorrow.) "Ali lahko plačam s kartico?" (Can I pay by card?) "Lahko noč" (good night) uses the same word.

Negatives: **ne morem** = I can't (from moči): "Ne morem priti." — but **ne moram** = I don't have to, **nočem** = ne + hočem (I don't want), **ni treba** = you don't have to: "Ni treba plačati."

The infinitive form never changes: "Mi moramo delati." "Ona hoče delati." Only the first verb changes for the person.

examples.text: Ne morem priti, ker sem bolan.
examples.en: I can't come because I'm ill.

points.title: Verbs with se: učim se, imenujem se
points.short: reflexive verbs with the little word se
points.explain:
Many Slovenian verbs come with the little word **se** ("oneself"). In English the meaning is often not reflexive at all — just learn **se** as part of the verb:
• **učiti se** — to learn: "Učim se slovensko."
• **imenovati se** — to be called: "Imenujem se Ana." (My name is Ana.)
• **veseliti se** — to look forward to: "Veselim se počitnic."
• **smejati se** — to laugh · **vrniti se** — to come back · **zgoditi se** — to happen

**Se never changes** for the person: učim se, učiš se, uči se, učimo se …

Its position is the tricky part: **se** is a short "clitic" that wants to stand in **second place** in the sentence, together with forms of "to be":
• "Učim se slovensko." (verb first, se second)
• "Jutri se učim." (jutri first, se second)
• "Kako se imenuješ?" (What's your name?)

When it meets "sem/si/je" in the past tense, se comes after them: "Učil sem se." / "Včeraj sem se učil."

points.title: The past: sem delal[a], si bil[a]
points.pattern: sem dela[l] · sem dela[la] · smo dela[li]
points.short: past tense = sem/si/je + the -l form
points.explain:
The Slovenian past tense has **one** form for "I worked / I was working / I have worked". It's made of **two parts**:
1. the present of **biti**: sem, si, je, smo, ste, so (sva, sta)
2. the **-l form** of the verb, which agrees with the **gender** of the person, like an adjective.

Make the -l form from the infinitive: remove **-ti**, add the ending:
• man: **-l** → dela[l], govori[l], bi[l]
• woman: **-la** → dela[la], govori[la], bi[la]
• neuter: **-lo** → bi[lo]
• plural: **-li** (m / mixed), **-le** (ž) · dual: **-la** (m), **-li** (ž)

Examples:
• "Včeraj sem dela[l]." (a man) / "Včeraj sem dela[la]." (a woman) — Yesterday I worked.
• "Kje si bi[l]?" — Where were you?
• "Bili smo na morju." — We were at the seaside.

**Iti** is irregular: šel, šla, šli. "Šel sem domov." (I went home.) Jesti → jedel, jedla.

Word order: the short "sem" goes to **second place**: "Včeraj **sem** bil doma.", but "Bil **sem** doma." Negation: **nisem** + -l form: "Nisem bil doma."

examples.en: Yesterday I worked at home. (a man)
In summer we were at the seaside.
Did you talk to mom? (to a woman)
Yesterday I went to the cinema. (a man)

points.title: The future: bom delal[a]
points.short: future = bom/boš/bo + the -l form
points.explain:
The future tense is easy once you know the past: use **bom** instead of **sem**, and the same -l form:
• (jaz) [bom] delal / delala — I will work
• (ti) [boš] delal(a)
• (on/ona) [bo] delal / delala
• (mi) [bomo] delali · (vi) [boste] delali · (oni) [bodo] delali
• dual: [bova], [bosta]

"Jutri **bom** delal." — Tomorrow I'll work. "Kaj **boš** jedel?" — What will you eat?

The future of **to be** is just bom / boš / bo … on their own: "Jutri **bom** doma." (Tomorrow I'll be at home.) "Kje **boš** jutri?"

**Iti** is special: in the future you say **bom šel / šla** — or, very commonly, just the present with a time word: "Jutri grem v Ljubljano." (Tomorrow I'm going to Ljubljana.) Slovenians use the present for plans just like English "I'm going …".

Negation: "Ne bom delal." (I won't work.) — here "ne" stays separate.

examples.en: What will you eat? (to a woman)
In summer we'll be at the seaside.

points.title: Do it! Pridi! Poglej[te]!
points.short: imperative: orders, requests, instructions
points.explain:
The **imperative** is used for requests and instructions: "Come!", "Look!", "Sit down, please." It's made from the **present** stem:
• **-am verbs** → **-aj**: delati → dela[j]!, čakati → čaka[j]!, poslušati → posluša[j]!
• **-im verbs** → **-i**: govoriti → govor[i]!, kupiti → kup[i]!
• **-em verbs** → **-i** (on the present stem): pisati → piš[i]!, brati → ber[i]!, priti → prid[i]!

For **vi** (several people, or polite), add **-te**: dela[jte], govor[ite], prid[ite], poglej[te], sed[ite]. For **we (let's)** add **-mo**: "Gremo!" "Pojdimo!" (Let's go!)

Some very common irregular ones: **iti** → pojdi! / pojdite! (or the everyday "greva / gremo"), **jesti** → jej!, **dati** → daj! ("Daj mi …" — Give me …), **imeti** → imej!

Add **prosim** to sound polite: "Prosim, sedite." (Please sit down.) "Počakajte, prosim." (Wait, please.)

Negative orders: ne + imperative: "Ne skrbi!" (Don't worry!) "Ne hodi tja!"

examples.en: Give me a glass of water.

points.title: Little words in second place
points.short: clitics (sem, se, mi, ga …) stand in second position
points.explain:
Slovenian word order is quite free — but one rule is strict: the **short unstressed words** (clitics) stand in **second place** in the sentence, right after the first word or phrase.

The clitics you know: forms of **biti** (sem, si, je, smo, ste, so, bom …), **se**, and short pronouns like **mi** (to me), **ti** (to you), **ga** (him/it), **jo** (her).

• "[Sem] doma." → "Danes **sem** doma." → "Danes zvečer **sem** doma." ("danes zvečer" counts as one first phrase)
• "Učim se." → "Jutri **se** učim."

When several clitics meet, they come in a fixed order: **biti** (except je) → **se** → dative (mi, ti) → accusative (ga, jo) → **je**:
• "Včeraj **sem se** učil." (I studied yesterday.)
• "Dal **sem mu ga**." (I gave it to him.)
• "Učil **se je**." (He studied — notice je comes last.)

You don't need to master this now. Just notice how sem / se like to be the second word — copying the example sentences out loud is the best way to get the feel for it.
